title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
excerpt: The argument from evil is the strongest case against God. Its older form claimed a contradiction and has been answered. Its newer form has not been refuted, and the Bible meets it with a man who was never told why and with a cross.
body:
A student meets the argument in a seminar room in her second year. It takes the professor four lines on a whiteboard, and she spends the walk home trying to find the flaw and can't. A man in his sixties has not been inside a church since the spring the river came through his town, because he could think of nothing a sermon might say that the water had not already answered. And a woman who still believes, and still prays, has grown tired of fellow Christians who explain her troubles to her. Each of them is asking why God allows evil. The student wants an argument answered. The man is past wanting an answer. The woman wants the explaining to stop.

This essay is mainly for the first of them, and it should say so. It weighs an argument. Nothing in it is offered as the reason for anything that has happened to you or to anyone you love.

If you're grieving as you read this, you don't have to resolve any of it before you're allowed to pray. Bring the question to God in whatever words you have; the psalms give you permission. Bring it to a person too, a friend or a pastor who will sit with you. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This essay can't counsel you, but [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call and a page for grief.

## The Old Form of the Argument

The question is older than Christianity. It has come down under the name of the Greek philosopher Epicurus, and David Hume gave it its best-known wording in 1779: "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?"

It is not a question the Bible is unaware of. Job puts it more bluntly than Hume did. "He destroys both the blameless and the wicked," he says of God, and when he looks at a world where judges are blind and the wicked hold the land, he asks, "if it is not he, who then is it?" (Job 9:22, 24).

In 1955 the philosopher J. L. Mackie turned the old question into a charge of contradiction. Believers hold three things, he said: God is all-powerful, God is wholly good, and evil exists. Two further principles seem to be built into the words themselves. Goodness gets rid of whatever evil it is able to, and omnipotence is able to do anything. Put those in, and the three cannot all be true. On this argument the believer does not merely lack evidence. His creed contradicts itself.

Mackie was right about several things, and Christians should say so. Evil is real. No sufferer has ever needed to be told so, and the Bible nowhere pretends otherwise. And the difficulty is sharpest for the believer, who will give up neither the goodness of God nor the badness of evil.

## The Answer From Freedom

The reply that met Mackie's argument is the oldest Christian reply in a careful modern form. A good being does not have to prevent every evil it could prevent. It may permit one if preventing it would cost a good that is greater. And there is a candidate for such a good, which is a world of creatures who are free in matters that count, able to love and so able to refuse. God can make free creatures. If he then causes them always to choose rightly, they are not choosing. So it is at least possible that a good and all-powerful God could not have a world with real love in it and no risk of real evil.

A charge of contradiction is answered by a single possibility, and this one was enough. Mackie granted, in a book published in 1982 after his death, that the problem of evil does not show the central claims of theism to be logically inconsistent. William Rowe, an atheist philosopher who pressed the problem as hard as anyone in the last century, wrote that no one had succeeded in showing that they are.

That is a real result and a small one, and the answer from freedom leaves a great deal unexplained. It does not explain why a God who values freedom doesn't stop the worst uses of it, as a good police officer would, without abolishing it. It has to face the Christian hope itself: if the redeemed will one day be free and never sin, it is fair to ask why God did not begin there. Reformed Christians, for the most part, define freedom differently and can't use the answer as it stands. They hold that God ordains all that happens and yet is not the author of sin. And it says nothing at all about the river. No human choice makes an earthquake or a cancer cell.

## The Stronger Form

Once the charge of contradiction had failed, the argument took a more modest shape, and the modest shape is the stronger one. It no longer says that God and evil can't both exist. It says that the evil we actually see makes God unlikely.

Rowe gave this form its classic statement in 1979 with one imagined case. Lightning strikes a dead tree in a distant forest and starts a fire. A fawn is caught in it, terribly burned, and lies in agony for days before it dies. No one sees it. Nobody is taught courage by it, no freedom is exercised, and no one is ever in a position to learn compassion from it. As far as anyone can tell, it serves no good at all. If even one such suffering is truly pointless, Rowe argued, then there is no being who is all-powerful, all-knowing and wholly good, because such a being would have prevented it.

Charles Darwin had felt the same weight more than a century earlier. In May of 1860 he wrote to his friend the botanist Asa Gray: "There seems to me too much misery in the world. I cannot persuade myself that a beneficent and omnipotent God would have designedly created the Ichneumonidae with the express intention of their feeding within the living bodies of Caterpillars, or that a cat should play with mice." He meant the wasps whose young eat their hosts alive from the inside.

Rowe did not claim to prove that the fawn's suffering is pointless. He reasoned as people reason every day: we look for a purpose, we find none, and we conclude that there probably isn't one. The longer treatment of [this argument](/questions/evil/the-evidential-problem-of-evil) on this site says that it "hasn't been refuted," and that is the fair description. Most of what it says should be granted. The suffering is real, and a great deal of it looks pointless from anywhere a human being can stand.

## Three More Answers, and Where Each Stops

The first further answer is that the world is a place for the making of persons. Irenaeus, a bishop in the second century, wrote that "it was possible for God Himself to have made man perfect from the first, but man could not receive this," being still, as he put it, "an infant." In 1966 the philosopher John Hick built that into a full account. Courage needs danger, compassion needs someone in pain, and faithfulness needs the chance to walk away. A world with no hazards in it might hold contented creatures. It could not hold grown ones.

This sees something true, and most people who have suffered and come through can point to what it sees. It stops short in three places. Much suffering does not form people. It breaks them. Some die too young for any forming to have begun, which is the subject of another essay on this site, on [why God lets children suffer](/writing/why-does-god-let-children-suffer). And the fawn's pain forms no one.

The second answer is that God permits evil because he brings out of it a good that could not have come another way. Augustine put it in a sentence: God "would never permit the existence of anything evil among His works, if He were not so omnipotent and good that He can bring good even out of evil." Christians who hold this point to the center of their own faith. Peter told a crowd in Jerusalem that Jesus was "delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God," and in the same sentence that "you crucified and killed" him "by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). For Christians the worst act in history and the saving of the world were one event.

This answer also stops. It can say that God brings good from evil. It cannot say what the good is in any given case, and the person who tries, at a bedside or a grave, has turned a confession into a cruelty. It also has to hear the objection that some goods are not worth their price, however great the good.

The third answer is about the limits of our sight. Not finding a reason counts against there being one only when the reason is the kind of thing we would expect to find. If there is a God, his purposes may run through centuries and through lives we know nothing of, and our failure to see them is about what we should expect either way. Darwin, to his credit, said something like this against himself in the same letter. "I feel most deeply that the whole subject is too profound for the human intellect," he wrote. "A dog might as well speculate on the mind of Newton."

This is the reply philosophers have argued over most since the 1980s, and it weakens Rowe's inference a good deal. Its cost is high. If God's reasons are hidden that completely, it becomes hard to say what his goodness means, or how anyone could tell it from its absence. And Rowe had a reply of his own. A loving God would at least assure the sufferer that there is a reason, as a parent stays in the room with a child who can't understand what is being done for him. Many people who suffer are given no such word.

As for the river, Christians have more than one account of why the natural world wounds its creatures. Some speak of a creation damaged by sin, and some of the regular laws that any world with living things in it would need. Scripture itself offers no mechanism. It says that the creation "was subjected to futility" and "has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:20, 22), which is to say that the world as it stands is not the world as it was meant to be or as it will be. A longer page on this site takes up [earthquakes, disease and the suffering of animals](/questions/evil/natural-evil-and-animal-suffering).

Each of the four answers has hold of something true. Taken together they show that the argument from evil is not a proof. None of them, and not all of them together, tells the man by the river why.

## The Book That Refuses

The Bible has a whole book on this question, and its method is to refuse explanations.

Within a few days Job's children are dead, his property is gone and his body is covered with sores. Three friends arrive, and after a week of silence, which is the best thing they do, they begin to explain. God is just, so suffering is deserved, so Job must have sinned. It is a tidy account of evil, and it is offered with Scripture and with concern. Job calls them "miserable comforters" and "worthless physicians" (Job 16:2; 13:4), and he goes on demanding a hearing from God himself.

When God speaks at last, he gives no reasons. He asks questions. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding" (Job 38:4). The book opens in heaven, with a scene that lies behind everything Job loses, and the reader sees it. Job never does. He receives the presence of God and no account of his suffering, and he says, "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5).

Then God turns to the friends, the men with the explanation, and tells them they "have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The man who accused God to his face is called truthful. The men who defended God with a theory are told to ask Job to pray for them. Whatever else that book does, it settles one thing for Christians. Nobody may walk into another person's suffering with the reason for it.

## What Christians Confess

The New Testament offers no theory of evil either. It offers an event, and what follows is a confession and should not be mistaken for a solution.

Christians confess that the God who would not explain himself to Job came into the world he made and suffered in it. Isaiah had spoken of "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3). At the grave of a friend, minutes before raising him, "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). On the cross he prayed the opening of a psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). The question the sufferer puts to God is found, in the Gospels, in the mouth of God's own Son.

They confess, too, that he was raised, and that evil is therefore something God means to end and has begun to end. Paul calls death "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26). That one word matters for this whole subject. Whatever good God brings out of evil, Scripture goes on calling evil and death his enemies. It never calls them his instruments and leaves it there.

To Rowe's question about why sufferers are given no assurance, the Christian reply is that an assurance was given, though not in the form of a reason: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). That reply will carry no weight with someone who doubts the history, and it does nothing for the fawn. It is a claim about what happened outside Jerusalem, and it has to be examined as history and can't be read off the amount of pain in the world.

We have often spoken as though we had more than this. We have told the bereaved that everything happens for a reason, and named the reason. We have told the sick that enough faith would have prevented it. We have defended God the way Job's friends did, and for the same motive, which is that an explained world is less frightening to the person doing the explaining.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that God is good and almighty, that evil is real and is the ruin of what he made, and that he is not its author. They confess that Christ suffered, died and rose, and that evil and death will end.

Whether God ordains the evils he does not prevent or only permits them, and which of the answers above carries the most weight, are questions on which faithful churches and teachers differ. This essay doesn't choose among them.

Why any particular evil was permitted is not known to anyone.

So the student has this to take back to the seminar. The four lines on the whiteboard do not show a contradiction, and the philosophers who pressed them hardest came to say so. The argument that replaced them is still standing, weakened and unrefuted. The man by the river has been given no reason, and the Bible is on his side in distrusting anyone who offers one. The woman who wanted the explaining to stop has a book of Scripture that stopped it. Darwin and Job ended in nearly the same words, that the matter was beyond them. The difference is that Job said it to someone, and believed he had been heard.

*"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding."* (Job 38:4)

*"The last enemy to be destroyed is death."* (1 Corinthians 15:26)
